paragraphs: R' Hanina bar Yaka, or Beruka, or bar Ika—Izka—Yasa.

Hyman records the following readings in the Yerushalmi: Berakhot ch. 9, end of halakha 2 (supplied: פ״ט סה״ב), R' Hanina bar Yaka says in the name of R' Yehuda: the roots of wheat penetrate the earth fifty cubits. The statement is cited in Avodah Zarah ch. 3, halakha 5, where it reads R' Hanina bar Yikha in the name of R' Yehuda; and in Taanit ch. 1, halakha 3, the statement is cited there as R' Hanina Beruka in the name of R' Yehuda. Likewise we find in Yevamot (supplied: פס״א) Rabbi Hanina Beruka in the name of Rabbi Yehuda: 'Concerning the people of Misha, no concern was raised about them,' etc.; and in Kiddushin ch. 4, halakha 1 (supplied: ה״א-לו.) it appears there as R' Hanina ben Beruka in the name of R' Yehuda. In Bereshit Rabbah at the end of ch. 13 the reading is R' Hanina bar Izka. Likewise it is mentioned in Beitzah ch. 1 end of halakhah 10 as Rav Hanina bar Yaka in the name of Rav Yehuda: one does not sift the flour a second time; and in Shabbat ch. 7, halakha 2 (supplied: כט.) the statement appears there as R' Hanina bar Yikha in the name of Rav Yehuda.
Likewise it is mentioned in Ketubot ch. 7, halakha 6: Hanina bar Ika in the name of R' Yehuda, 'and in all of them, if she brought proof for her words, she is believed.'
From all these readings it appears to Hyman that he was a student of Rav Yehuda, and he is not R' Hanina son of Rav Ika, who lived in the time of Rava and also after him.

notes.text: אין שונין את הקמח means not sifting flour a second time, not grinding it. The supplied name/title variants and Hyman’s distinction from the later Chanina son of Rav Ika remain explicit. The incomplete Yevamot locator and phrase בני מישא retain a source-research hold.

The whole saved Guggenheimer Jerusalem Talmud Yevamot1:6 scalar, text index6 (789 characters), was read and checked against its raw SHA256, selector and actual edition metadata. It explicitly reads Rabbi Haninah Beroka in the name of Rabbi Yehudah, followed by בני מישא לא חשו להו אלא משם ספק חללות. This supports concern ABOUT the people of Misha, not the people of Misha worrying about other people. Hyman's supplied quotation stops at לא חשו להו/etc; the digital continuation restricts the concern to doubtful chalal status, but that unsupplied qualification and the rest of the genealogy/geography discussion are not imported into the translated body or admitted as population facts. Misha is retained without equating it with Mesene or binding a town identity. The source פס״א remains verbatim in the English locator label; the saved1:6 comparison and a contextual END chapter1 interpretation do not prove that Hyman printed ספ״א, authorize swapping the letters or settle a correction history. The local full Rabbi titles support only the two named Yevamot reporting occurrences; they do not expand the heading, Berakhot/Avodah Zarah/Taanit/Kiddushin/BR/Shabbat/Ketubot citations or the later namesake. Abbreviated unsupported titles stay R'; all explicit full Rav occurrences in Beitzah, Shabbat and Hyman's final student/namesake distinction remain Rav. The supplied יקא Yaka and יכא Yikha remain distinct, as do איקא Ika and עיקא Ayka, Izka איזקא, Yasa יסא, Beruka ברוקה and ben Beruka בן ברוקה; Beruka is not automatically split into bar and a father's name. Earlier Ayka for איקא and repeated Yaka for יכא remain archived exactly, without harmonization, identity merger or inferred genealogy. Hanina in the body and Chanina in the title remain distinct transliterations. The digital Haninah/Beroka forms are local witness forms, not replacements for Hyman. FIFTY CUBITS, wheat ROOTS PENETRATE THE EARTH and each speaker REPORTS Yehuda retain their source force without a new botanical claim. Berakhot9 END halakhah2 restores the END component of supplied סה״ב; Beitzah1 END halakhah10 and BR END13 likewise retain END, not arbitrary ranges or modern numbering proof. Kiddushin4hal1 plus suppliedלו. and Shabbat6hal2 plusכט. retain the unsided numerals; all other locator mappings remain conventional. The earlier no-grinding reading stays archived; current NO SECOND SIFTING remains the inherited lexical interpretation of אין שונין את הקמח, not a freshly read Beitzah/Shabbat witness or a new law. Untitled Ketubot Hanina remains untitled; ALL OF THEM/IF SHE BROUGHT PROOF/FOR HER WORDS/SHE IS BELIEVED retains conditional and feminine force, with וכילהן a disclosed contextual approximation. Hyman's FROM ALL THESE READINGS/IT APPEARS student inference remains tentative and expressly attributed. His NOT THIS Hanina son of Rav Ika distinction, Rava's time AND ALSO AFTER HIM retain their full force as his source claims, without admitting chronology or reconciling the namesakes. All three original mixed notes, current mixed note, all English histories and root intermediate changes remain exact. The proposed source resolution, body-locator replacement, added legal/geographic continuation and current-note revision are not applied; only this qualification is appended and p002 stays held, without publication, Hebrew repair or semantic/authority admission.

The whole printed notice is in volume II, pp. 492–493. Its Shabbat and Ketubot references have chapter 7, beside chapter 6 in the frozen Hebrew. The English follows those printed chapters; the supplied Hebrew and all existing notes remain unchanged. The corresponding whole Guggenheimer passages are Shabbat 7:2 and Ketubot 7:6. The former has Hanina ben Yake in the name of Rav Yehudah, while Beitzah 1:10 has bar Yake; both concern sifting flour again, not grinding. Their additional discussion about the back of the sieve is not inserted into Hyman’s abridgement. The printed Bereshit Rabbah name is bar Izka (בר עיזקא), beside the frozen bar Ayka (בר עיקא); this is a witness difference, not a new identification. The whole Berakhot 9:2 and Taanit 1:3 texts have bar Yakka/Yake in the name of Rav Yehudah; Avodah Zarah 3:5 has bar Yasa in the name of Rav Yehudah. These differ from several readings and Rabbi/Rav titles reported by Hyman. Yevamot 1:6 has Hanina Beroka in the name of Rabbi Yehudah; Kiddushin 4:1 has Hanina ben Beroka in the name of Rav Yehudah. Both discuss concern about the people of Misha on account of doubtful chalal status; the fuller qualification and geographic discussion are not inserted into Hyman’s shortened quotation, nor adopted as population facts or a town identification. The printed פס״א is left literal alongside this Yevamot comparison. Ketubot 7:6 has Hanina bar Ika, in the name of Rabbi Yehudah, and the conditional statement about proof for her words; the English commentary calls it an explanation for her conduct. This does not turn the translation into a legal ruling. The forms Yaka, Yikha, Ika, Izka, Yasa and Beruka, and bar versus ben, remain distinct witnesses. Hyman’s inference that he studied under Rav Yehudah, and his exclusion of the later Hanina son of Rav Ika, remain his historical argument, not an admitted identity or chronology. Other exact editions have not been independently collated here. The retained notes describe earlier review stages; their pending-source statements are preserved as that record, alongside the new comparisons above.
